what: The Transliteration Tool rewrites text from other writing systems in Latin letters, so you can read names, addresses and words you cannot type or pronounce.

It supports Cyrillic, Greek, Arabic (with Persian and Urdu letters), Hebrew, Devanagari, Thai, Korean Hangul, Japanese hiragana and katakana, Chinese, Georgian and Armenian, using standard systems such as ISO 9, ALA-LC, ICAO passport style, ELOT 743, IAST, ISO 15919, Revised Romanization, Hepburn, Kunrei-shiki and Hanyu Pinyin.
It runs in your browser; only Chinese needs a small extra download the first time.
uses: Write a Russian, Greek or Arabic name or address in Latin letters for a form, ticket or parcel.
See how words in a new alphabet are pronounced while you learn it.
Romanize titles and names with ALA-LC, ISO 9 or ISO 15919.
Read signs, menus and place names you copied from the web.
Make Latin-letter versions of names so they can be searched and sorted.
tutorial: Type or paste text in any of the supported scripts, or click an example.
The Latin version appears as you type. Each script in the text is detected and converted on its own.
Only the settings for scripts in your text are shown. For Cyrillic, pick the language and a system: simple/national, passport (ICAO), library (ALA-LC) or ISO 9.
For Japanese choose Hepburn or Kunrei and how long vowels are written; for Chinese choose tone marks, numbers or none.
Tick Plain ASCII output for letters without any marks, such as for email addresses or file names.
features: Mixed text, such as a Russian name in an English sentence, is converted piece by piece.
ISO 9, ALA-LC, ICAO 9303, ELOT 743, ISO 843, IAST, ISO 15919, Revised Romanization, Hepburn, Kunrei-shiki and Hanyu Pinyin.
Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Bulgarian, Serbian and Macedonian each follow their own rules.
Korean liaison and nasal assimilation, Japanese small tsu and long vowels, Greek αυ/ευ and μπ, Arabic al- and shadda.
Characters with several readings are chosen from the words around them.
Notes appear for scripts that need care, such as Arabic without vowels or Japanese kanji.

example.title: A Ukrainian address
example.text: Paste Київ, вулиця Хрещатик. With Cyrillic language set to Ukrainian and the simple (national) system you get Kyiv, vulytsia Khreshchatyk, the official Ukrainian romanization. With ISO 9 you get Kiïv, vulicâ Hreŝatik instead.

tips: Set the right Cyrillic language: г is g in Russian but h in Ukrainian.
For passports and visas, use the Passport (ICAO 9303) system and compare with your document.
Add vowel marks to Arabic or Hebrew text for a more complete reading.
Write Japanese kanji words in kana to convert them.
problems: Arabic is normally written without short vowels. Only text with vowel marks (harakat) can be fully converted.
Kanji readings depend on the word and need a dictionary. Hiragana and katakana are converted.
A Thai word looks slightly different from the official spelling
Thai does not always write vowels or syllable breaks, so the rule-based RTGS conversion can differ for some words.
